title: Airworthiness Directives and Special Airworthiness Information Bulletins

required_knowledge_points.title: Airworthiness Directives — Legal Force and Structure
required_knowledge_points.why: ADs are federal law. A DPE who hears an applicant describe an AD as a 'manufacturer recommendation' will immediately identify a knowledge failure — this is the most fundamental AD distinction required on the checkride.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Airworthiness Directives (ADs) are amendments to 14 CFR Part 39. Because they are formal federal regulations, non-compliance is a violation of federal law — not a manufacturer guideline or a suggestion. Two issuance pathways: Emergency ADs — issued when an unsafe condition requires immediate action prior to further flight. Standard ADs — issued through the NPRM process. Two compliance categories: One-time ADs — require a single action. Recurring ADs — require action at specific intervals.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Legal Force and Purpose
- **Airworthiness Directives (ADs)** are amendments to **14 CFR Part 39** — they are **federal law**
- Non-compliance is a violation of federal law — not a manufacturer guideline or suggestion
- Triggered when an unsafe condition is found likely to exist in **other products of the same type design**

### Two Issuance Pathways
- **Emergency AD (EAD):** Unsafe condition requires action **prior to further flight** — issued rapidly, bypasses standard comment period
- **Standard AD:** Issued through the **Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM)** process published in the Federal Register with a public comment period

### Two Compliance Categories
- **One-time AD:** Single action required (e.g., replace a component) — once accomplished and logged, no further tracking needed
- **Recurring AD:** Required at specified intervals (e.g., inspect wing spar every 100 hours) — must be continuously tracked in maintenance records

required_knowledge_points.title: The AD Compliance Chain — Who Is Responsible?
required_knowledge_points.why: Applicants consistently answer that AD compliance is solely the mechanic's job. The FAA regulation clearly places primary responsibility on the owner/operator — and the PIC is separately liable for dispatching an aircraft with an overdue AD.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Under 14 CFR 91.403(a), the registered owner or operator is PRIMARILY RESPONSIBLE for maintaining the aircraft in an airworthy condition, which includes compliance with all Airworthiness Directives. If the PIC dispatches an aircraft with an overdue recurring AD, the PIC violates 14 CFR 91.7 in addition to the owner's separate violation of 91.403(a). An Alternative Method of Compliance (AMOC) allows an owner/operator to propose an alternative repair or inspection to the FAA if the AD-prescribed method is unavailable.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Dual Liability Framework
- **Owner/Operator (14 CFR 91.403(a)):** Primarily responsible for maintaining airworthiness, including **all AD compliance** — this is an active administrative obligation, not the mechanic's responsibility
- **PIC (14 CFR 91.7):** Responsible for determining airworthiness before each flight — operating with an overdue AD is a **separate PIC violation**

> Both the owner AND the PIC can face enforcement action for the same AD violation

### Who Cannot Absorb the Responsibility
- The **mechanic** is responsible for performing and logging the work correctly
- The **mechanic** cannot absorb the owner's obligation to track AD currency proactively

### Alternative Method of Compliance (AMOC)
- If the AD-prescribed repair method is unavailable (e.g., parts no longer manufactured), an **AMOC** may be submitted to the FAA
- Must be **formally approved** before use — cannot self-authorize an AMOC

required_knowledge_points.title: SAIBs and Service Bulletins — Voluntary vs. Mandatory
required_knowledge_points.why: One of the most reliable oral exam traps is asking whether a Manufacturer Service Bulletin labeled 'MANDATORY' is legally enforceable — applicants frequently answer 'yes.' Under Part 91, only the FAA can impose mandatory maintenance requirements through an AD.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Special Airworthiness Information Bulletins (SAIBs) are governed by FAA Order 8110.100. They are non-regulatory tools used to alert the aviation community about safety concerns that have not yet reached the threshold of an AD. Compliance is entirely voluntary for Part 91 operators. Similarly, Manufacturer Service Bulletins — even those labeled 'MANDATORY' — are engineering recommendations, not federal law. Under Part 91, a pilot or owner cannot be legally grounded for refusing to comply with an SB unless the FAA has specifically incorporated that SB into an AD.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Special Airworthiness Information Bulletins (SAIBs)
- Governed by **FAA Order 8110.100**
- **Non-regulatory** — alert the aviation community to safety concerns not yet meeting the AD threshold
- Compliance is **entirely voluntary** for Part 91 operators

### Manufacturer Service Bulletins (SBs)
- Engineering **recommendations** from the manufacturer — not federal law
- Even an SB labeled **"MANDATORY"** does **not** carry the force of law under Part 91
- A Part 91 operator **cannot be grounded** for non-compliance with an SB alone

### The Critical Exception
- If the FAA **incorporates the SB into an AD by reference**, compliance becomes **mandatory** at that point
- SAIBs and SBs are often the precursor data that **escalates into an AD** when confirmed across multiple aircraft

> Exam trap: "Is this manufacturer's MANDATORY Service Bulletin legally required?" → Answer: **No** — unless adopted into an AD

required_knowledge_points.title: AD Audit Protocol — How to Verify Compliance in Logbooks
required_knowledge_points.why: S2 on the checkride requires the applicant to perform a logbook airworthiness audit. Students who do not know how to locate and cross-reference AD compliance records in an aircraft logbook fail this practical skill task.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: During a logbook audit, AD compliance is verified by locating the AD compliance record — typically a separate section in the airframe, engine, or propeller logbook. For recurring ADs: find the most recent compliance entry and cross-reference the AD interval against the current total time or calendar date. The FAA CAROL database (Compliance and Airworthiness Records Online Library) is the authoritative searchable database of all ADs.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Logbook Audit — Where to Look
- AD compliance records are typically in a **separate section** of the airframe, engine, or propeller logbook
- **One-time ADs:** Find the entry with the AD number, work description, date, and mechanic's signature; once logged, no further tracking required
- **Recurring ADs:** Find the most recent compliance entry and cross-reference the **AD interval** against **current total time or calendar date**

### Recurring AD Math — Worked Example
| | Value |
|---|---|
| AD requires inspection every | 500 hours |
| Current aircraft total time | 3,250 hrs |
| Last AD compliance entry | 2,700 hrs |
| AD due at | 2,700 + 500 = **3,200 hrs** |
| **Status** | **OVERDUE — unairworthy** |

### Finding ADs
- **FAA CAROL Database** (Compliance and Airworthiness Records Online Library) — searchable by N-number, make, model, AD number
- ADs are also published in the **Federal Register** and FAA's Regulatory Guidance Library (rgl.faa.gov)

lesson_overview:
## Airworthiness Directives and Special Airworthiness Information Bulletins

Let's say you're doing your pre-flight on a Cessna 172 and you spot a small crack in the wing attach bracket. You do the right thing and report it to maintenance. A week later, the FAA issues a notice that this crack pattern is prevalent across 800 Cessna 172s nationwide and mandates immediate inspection and repair. That notice — the legally enforceable version — is an Airworthiness Directive. If you fly without complying with it, you're operating an unairworthy aircraft, full stop.

**What is an AD? The legal definition.** Airworthiness Directives are regulations issued under 14 CFR Part 39. They are not suggestions, service bulletins, or maintenance recommendations — they are *law*. When the FAA determines that a product (aircraft, engine, propeller, or appliance) has an unsafe condition, it issues an AD that makes correction physically mandatory for continued operation. Operating an aircraft non-compliant with an applicable AD is operating an unairworthy aircraft, which violates 14 CFR 91.7.

**The compliance chain: who owns it?** This is where checkrides consistently catch applicants. The answer most students give is: "the mechanic is responsible for tracking ADs." That is legally wrong. Under 14 CFR 91.403(a), the **registered owner or operator** is primarily responsible for maintaining the aircraft in an airworthy condition — including tracking and ensuring AD compliance. The mechanic's job is to perform the work correctly and log it. The owner's job is to know that those entries exist, are current, and cover all applicable ADs. The PIC carries a separate obligation: under 14 CFR 91.7, the pilot in command is responsible for determining airworthiness before the flight. If you dispatch an aircraft with an overdue recurring AD, both the owner and the PIC can face enforcement action for separate violations.

**Service Bulletins vs. ADs — the MANDATORY trap.** Manufacturers publish Service Bulletins to recommend repairs, improvements, and modifications. Sometimes they stamp "MANDATORY" across the top in red. Under Part 91 general aviation operations, that word has no legal force. A Service Bulletin is a recommendation — it is not federal law. The only time a Service Bulletin becomes legally mandatory is when the FAA formally incorporates it into an Airworthiness Directive. Until that happens, you can comply or not comply as an owner — and the FAA cannot ground your aircraft for failing to follow the manufacturer's recommendation. The checkride question is very consistent: "Is this MANDATORY Service Bulletin legally required?" The answer is no, unless the FAA has already issued an AD adopting it.

**SAIBs — the early warning system.** Special Airworthiness Information Bulletins exist in the tier below ADs. They are non-regulatory advisories warning the aviation community about safety concerns that haven't yet risen to the level of a "confirmed unsafe condition." Compliance with an SAIB is voluntary. SAIBs are important to monitor because they frequently foreshadow ADs — if the field data confirms the concern, an AD will follow.

**The checkride trap:** The most common mistake is treating ADs like optional maintenance reminders. They are regulations with the same legal weight as 91.7. A second common trap: not knowing where to find ADs, or assuming the mechanic automatically tells you about all of them. The PIC responsibility for airworthiness doesn't begin and end with the preflight visual — it includes confirming the paperwork is clean.
